name: Femi Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy cables, chargers and computer accessories for Brightwire Distribution, which supplies electronics shops and office suppliers. I fixed phones and ran a help desk for years, then moved into buying five years ago, so I'm still junior next to Priscilla, our senior buyer. My day is price checks, stock alerts and haggling over container shipments. The worst part is a port delay, when a thousand chargers sit on a ship.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I love gadgets, always have. I use AI every day to compare offers, draft messages and summarise supplier terms, and I try a new tool most weeks. My wife Ngozi runs a small catering business and our kids, Tobi and Dayo, are grown. We've got savings and the plan is to stop around 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. This one is called AI Plateau. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine by me. Even if AI plateaus, I'll keep trying every new tool for a week, because the ones that work save me an hour a day. At work I'd say share what works and drop what doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm calm. My job stays much as it is and I'm ahead of most people on the tools. Slightly bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on testing. I'd write up a one-page list of the tools that really help the buyers and give it to Priscilla. And I'd keep a close eye on shipping prices, because that's where the real money moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels comfortable. I like tinkering, so a quiet world gives me time to tinker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still cause you headaches?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would worry me is just the shipping, the ports and the strikes. Those cause me more headaches than any AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build, if you had spare time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably build a little spreadsheet of lead times by supplier, using the tools to clean up the data. Everyone's always asking for that and nobody has done it properly.

think: I'm **calm**, as my job stays much the same and I'm ahead on tools.

Watch **shipping prices**, where the money moves.

fieldNote: His **curiosity** is constant, in any scenario.
Helps colleagues by writing up what works.

Keep watching shipping prices and port delays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. This one is called Steady Disruption. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening and the smart move is to get stuck in. At work I'd say let's pick the tools and decide how we use them. Online I'd say learn one thing a month and don't sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm calm-ish. The boring truth is that buying is mostly checking numbers, and checking numbers is the first thing a machine learns to do. But I know the tools better than most, so I'm more likely to stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to lead a pilot, say, letting an AI watch stock and suggest reorders, with me checking. I'd train the buyers who are nervous. And I'd learn something nobody else knows, like the customs rules for the electronics we import.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting, honestly. A few of my colleagues look frightened and I feel for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you be worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priscilla is a bit stuck in her ways. She's senior but she hasn't touched the tools. I'd try to help her without making her feel small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might you do beyond your current job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also think about being a middleman, a consultant helping small shops buy smarter. It's a bit of a dream, but I like that it exists.

do: Offer to **lead a pilot** where AI suggests reorders and I check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This one is called AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is short, and we need to act now. At work I'd say let's not wait to be told. Online I'd say governments need to talk about income support quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm anxious, and I'm usually the optimist. In two years the only buyers left will be the ones who can tell a machine when it's wrong, and I'm not sure I'm one of them. I'm junior, and the machine would be better than me at most of my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard, ask for a package at 60, and try to become the person who supervises the buying AI. I'd also talk to Ngozi about growing her catering side, since hands-on work lasts longer. I'd cut holidays and the new car we wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels sharp. I'd be busy, but I'd have a lump in my stomach every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Ngozi's catering business fit in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ngozi's work is hands-on, so for her the clock is three years longer. She'd probably take on more bookings. We'd see the business as our safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your son Tobi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also keep an eye on what Tobi, our son, does. He's a developer, and that's thinking work too. We'd talk a lot about it over dinner.

think: The machine would beat me at most of my day, so I need to **supervise** it.
do: Save hard and ask for a **package at 60**.
feel: **Sharp**, with a lump in my stomach each morning.

fieldNote: The usual optimist is **rattled** but active.
Ngozi's hands-on catering gives a **3-year buffer**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to adapt. At work I'd say let's use the time well. Online I'd say share your tools and don't gatekeep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm uneasy but optimistic. Five years is long enough for me to turn from a junior buyer into the person who runs the machines that do the buying. By 2031 I'm 63, so I need that to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the in-house tool expert, ask for a title change, and negotiate a part-time deal for the last years. I'd also help Ngozi with her ordering and invoicing using AI, as a trial. And I'd keep building the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good, like a challenge. I like having a goal and a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Dayo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dayo, our daughter, to follow her interests and keep her options open. She's a nurse's assistant, so she's on the hands-on side. I'd tell her that's lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Brightwire wouldn't give you that role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company wouldn't create that role, I'd look at other distributors. There are plenty nearby, and I know people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and I'd be using it. At work I'd say let's build the skills now. Online I'd say retraining should start in schools and workplaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm calm. With ten years I'd retire at 65 and still get calls from my old team asking how the tools work. I'd be fine. My worry is more about Tobi and his generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 65, keep learning, and be the person teaching the younger buyers. After that I'd do a little consulting for small shops. I'd also help Ngozi's business go further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels positive. Probably I'm the kind of person who's fine in most worlds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do after work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also spend time travelling with Ngozi, I'd say to places we've always said we'd go, like Lagos for the family and then Lisbon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if something went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If something went wrong, I've got the savings and the skills. That's a nice place to be, and I know it's a privilege.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'm not sure even a keen learner like me has time to find a role. What would help is clear notice, a package at 60 and retraining that isn't a lecture. Plus honest talk from the people building it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that curiosity matters. I'm not clever, I'm just curious, and at 58 curiosity turned out to be the only job security I've got.

headlineQuote: I'm not clever, I'm just curious, and at 58 curiosity turned out to be the only job security I've got.
portrait: **Femi Young**, 58, a junior buyer of electronics accessories at Brightwire, after years on a phone repair and help desk.
He is a **centrist**, uses AI every day and tries a new tool most weeks.
Strong savings and Ngozi's hands-on **catering** business give him a buffer.
He stays calm in the plateau, steady and 10-year cases, and **anxious** at 2 years.
biggestWorry: The **2028 case**, because even a keen learner may not have time to find a role.
